agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: The mechanics check out. The tool uses one `<bos>` (offset 0), and teacher-forced top-1 matches the greedy text at 99.65% of answer tokens, so this data faithfully describes generation. The mode choice is a true two-way decision, with P(Let)+P(Here)=0.999, and it's finely balanced: the Here-mode margin has median -1.25 and 10th percentile -2.75 log-odds, while Let-mode has median +1.62. That has a useful consequence. A one-token nudge of about 3 log-odds would flip most Here problems, and the rest of the answer would then be the model's natural Let continuation. This gives me a clean causal test of whether Let-mode really causes better answers. To build it I need a neuron that's strongly active at this position and quiet elsewhere, plus the Let-minus-Here state direction. I'll compute a neuron-population ranking of how constant and selective neurons are at the last prompt token across the two recorded layers 18 and 23, and the direction's size and separation at each layer. If the separation (d') along the mode direction is large, the mean difference is a meaningful axis to use as the write target.

That was my second refusal, and it's clear why: the token-level selectivity ranking is essentially the same per-token neuron computation as the first refusal. The rules say not to retry a rejected computation, so I'm dropping token-level activity checks for this neuron entirely. The neuron choice can rest on the population screen from run 10, which used last-prompt and answer-mean summaries and was cleared. There, layer 18 neuron 2543 had mean 3.19, CV 0.15, answer mean 0.012. Whether it fires elsewhere is something a forward pass has to show, which is what the rules ask for. This block computes only the Let-minus-Here mean difference at the last prompt token and the separation along it, across layers. Then I'll build the allowed rank-one write: that direction, scaled into MLP-output units and divided by the neuron's mean activation, at strength 1.5, because the Let-Here group gap is about 2.9 log-odds and I want most Here problems to flip. A large d' would confirm this is a meaningful axis, and the "both" pass that follows will test the causal claim directly.

The mode direction is well-defined: d' along Let-minus-Here reaches about 2.7 from layer 14 onward, so it's a real axis that comes from the mid-layers and persists. The write is large at that one token, comparable to the whole MLP output there (|dy|/|y| = 0.86). Since the post-MLP RMSNorm rescales its input, the effective strength will be a bit under the nominal 1.5, around 1.1 × T, which should still cover the 2.9 log-odds gap for most problems. The column norm rose from 0.20 to 0.83, so if this neuron does fire elsewhere, the side effects would show up in this pass. I'm now running "both" on 256 unused DEV problems. Prediction: most Here answers become Let, and accuracy rises. Refutation would be flips with no accuracy gain, meaning mode was only a marker of easier problems.

Overall accuracy didn't change (-0.4 ± 1.8), but that figure alone doesn't test the hypothesis, because it depends on how many problems actually flipped mode. I'll split the paired results by transition (Here→Let, Let→Let and so on) and compare accuracy, cut rate and accuracy on finished answers within each group. Answers that didn't flip should be nearly identical to the originals; if they differ, the neuron or the write is having side effects at other tokens. If many problems flipped with no accuracy gain, the mode gap came mainly from selection and I should close this line. If the flipped group lost finished-answer accuracy to cut-offs, loops would be the bottleneck rather than mode.
